body.hook: Fifty musicians, one person waving a baton, and everyone plays at exactly the same moment. That's the magic of following a conductor, and the conductor's patterns are a language you can learn.

study.title: Reading the Baton
study.question: How do I follow a conductor?
study.passage:
Conducting patterns (written for this lesson):
4/4: down (1), left (2), right (3), up (4).
3/4: down (1), right (2), up (3).
2/4: down (1), up (2).
The downbeat (beat 1) always goes down; the last beat always goes up.
Preparatory beat: the conductor raises the baton and gives one beat before playing; breathe in with it and play on the next downbeat.
Activities: 1. Everyone conducts each pattern with the right hand while counting aloud. 2. Student conductors lead the class saying "ta" on each beat; others follow. 3. Tempo changes: the conductor speeds up and slows down; players follow. 4. Eyes: practise reading a line while glancing up at the conductor at the end of each bar. Tip: put your stand so you can see the conductor just over the top of the music.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; patterns follow standard conducting practice.

body.objective: Students will be able to start and release together.
body.iCan: I can start and release together.
successCriteria: I can breathe and start together on the conductor's cue

body.hook: Nothing sounds more professional than a band starting and stopping perfectly together, and nothing sounds messier than notes trickling in and out. Clean starts and releases are a team skill.

vocabulary.definition: The moment a player or section starts playing.
Ending a note together, also called a cut-off.

A sign (𝄐) telling players to hold a note until the conductor releases it.

study.title: Start and Stop Together
study.question: How does a band start and release notes together?
study.passage:
Together drills (written for this lesson):
1. Breath together: on the preparatory beat, everyone breathes in with the conductor's arm. Air ready = clean attack.
2. Attack drill: conductor gives a prep beat; band plays Concert B♭ on the downbeat. Repeat until the attack sounds like one instrument.
3. Fermata drill: hold Concert F under a fermata; the conductor holds as long as they like. Release on the cut-off gesture (a small loop that closes, or a closing hand).
4. Release on a beat: hold a whole note and release exactly on beat 1 of the next bar (the "release on the next downbeat" rule), unless the conductor shows otherwise.
5. Section matching: each section plays a four-bar line; others listen for ragged starts or endings.
Tips: keep air steady to the end of each note; stop the sound with the end of the air, not with your tongue slamming shut.

body.objective: Students will be able to listen to match the band.
body.iCan: I can listen to match the band.
successCriteria: I can listen to other players while I play
I can match my section's volume and note lengths
I can describe how my part fits the whole band
body.hook: In a band you're not a soloist; you're part of a team sound. The secret is listening more than you play: matching the people around you in pitch, volume and note length.

vocabulary.definition: A group of musicians performing together.
Players of the same instrument, such as the clarinet section.
The lowest part, often played by tuba, bass clarinet or bassoon.
Listening to yourself, then your section, then the whole band.

study.title: Listen and Match
study.question: How do I fit my sound into the band?
study.passage:
Listening ladder (written for this lesson):
Step 1, me: Can I hear my own steady tone?
Step 2, my section: Can I hear the players beside me? If I hear only myself, I'm too loud.
Step 3, the band: Can I hear the melody? The bass? If the melody is buried, accompanying parts play softer.
Activities: 1. Section relay: each section plays Concert B♭ for 4 counts in turn; then all together. Could you still hear each section? 2. Volume match: one section plays at mf; the next must match. 3. Who has the melody? Play a simple band arrangement (e.g. a chorale); after each phrase, raise hands if you think you had the melody. 4. Bass-up: start a chord with low brass and low woodwinds, then add middle, then high instruments. The band sounds best built from the bottom up. 5. Reflect: describe your part's job: melody, harmony, bass or rhythm.
